message.content:
{
  "frontend": {
    "needed": true,
    "prompt": "Shared explicit contract facts (repeat of requirement):
- Restore the superuser role's ability to modify and delete other users' entries (only this permission change).
- Remove read-only error messages and UI restrictions that prevent that role from editing/deleting others' entries.
- Ordinary/regular users accessing other users' resources must still receive 404; under no circumstances may this behavior be changed to returning 403.
- Superuser read-all behavior must remain unchanged (superusers continue to be able to read all resources as before).
- Scope is limited to implementing only the above; do not invent or assume any other historical or unspecified behavioral changes.

Frontend-specific omissions (explicit):
- The requirement does NOT supply the exact frontend role identifier string, auth state shape, component/file paths, routing names, localization keys, or framework-specific APIs. Do not assume names; locate them in the codebase before changing code.
- The requirement does NOT specify whether buttons are hidden via CSS, conditional rendering, or feature flags—inspect implementation before modifying.

Required tasks for frontend implementation:
1) Locate UI code that enforces read-only UI for the superuser role on other users' entries. This may include: disabling or hiding edit/delete buttons, showing a read-only banner or error, or blocking UI actions client-side. Identify the exact condition(s) checking role + ownership.
2) Change the UI condition so that users with the superuser role are NOT subject to the read-only UI restrictions for entries owned by other users. Specifically, ensure edit and delete controls are rendered and enabled for the superuser when viewing others' entries.
3) Remove or update any client-side logic that displays a read-only error message for the superuser role when viewing others' entries. Keep other error messages intact (do not remove messages that apply to regular users).
4) Keep the UI behavior for ordinary/regular users unchanged: the UI should still hide/disable edit/delete controls (or otherwise behave as before) when a regular user views another user's resource.
5) Do NOT change any client-side behavior that converts or interprets backend 404 responses into 403s or other statuses. If the frontend maps 404 to alternative UI, do not alter that mapping unless it is a mapping that incorrectly converts to 403 for regular users; in that case, ensure the mapping preserves 404 semantics (but do not alter server-side status codes).
6) Add or update frontend tests (unit and integration/UI tests) covering these cases:
   - Superuser viewing another user's entry: edit and delete controls are visible and actionable; attempts to perform edit/delete send requests to backend.
   - Regular user viewing another user's entry: UI remains read-only as before; requests (if UI allows attempt) should be expected to receive 404 from backend.
   - Superuser reading resources: reading behavior unchanged.
7) Ensure that when the frontend sends modify/delete requests for superuser-initiated actions, it properly handles success (200/204) and existing error responses. Do not alter error handling to treat 404 as 403.
8) Coordinate with backend implementer to ensure the backend will accept modify/delete from superuser before enabling any UI that allows those actions in production; plan for a synchronized deploy or a guarded feature flag to avoid enabled UI pointing at a backend that still rejects the action.

Acceptance criteria for frontend (must be verifiable):
- When logged in as superuser and viewing another user's entry, edit and delete controls are visible and enabled; executing them issues requests to backend.
- When logged in as a regular user and viewing another user's entry, UI remains read-only as before; there is no change to how 404 responses are handled.
- No UI path converts 404 responses for other-users' resources into 403 responses.
- No read-only banner/error remains for the superuser when viewing others' entries.

Notes to implementer (do not assume):
- Before making changes, identify exact role name/claim used in auth state and confirm with backend if necessary; do not hardcode a guessed role string.
- Do not remove or change UI controls for other roles unless explicitly required by the code inspection and consistent with the requirement.
- Do not change or infer any server endpoint names or response formats; rely on existing API contracts and coordinate with backend developer for discrepancies."
  },
  "backend": {
    "needed": true,
    "prompt": "Shared explicit contract facts (repeat of requirement):
- Restore the superuser role's ability to modify and delete other users' entries (only this permission change).
- Remove read-only errors targeted at that role (i.e., server-side errors that prevent that role from editing/deleting others' entries) and any server-side interface-level restrictions for that role.
- Ordinary/regular users accessing other users' resources must still receive 404; under no circumstances may this be changed to 403.
- Superuser read-all behavior must remain unchanged (superusers continue to be able to read all resources as before).
- Scope is limited to implementing only the above; do not invent or assume any other historical or unspecified behavioral changes.

Backend-specific omissions (explicit):
- The requirement does NOT provide exact code locations, role identifier strings, middleware names, auth library, route/endpoint names, or model names. Do not assume these; locate them in the codebase before editing.
- The requirement does NOT specify whether ownership checks are performed in middleware, per-handler code, ORM hooks, or policy files—inspect and update the right layer accordingly.

Required tasks for backend implementation:
1) Locate all authorization checks that block modify (PATCH/PUT) and delete (DELETE) operations on resources owned by other users. This includes middleware, controller/handler code, policy classes, authorization decorators, or composition filters.
2) Modify the authorization logic so that users with the superuser role are permitted to perform modify and delete operations on entries owned by other users. Make the change only in the specific authorization check(s) that control modify/delete operations on other-users' resources; do not broaden other permissions.
3) Ensure read (GET) behavior for superusers remains unchanged. Do not alter any read-path logic that currently grants superusers full read access.
4) Preserve the existing behavior for ordinary/regular users: when they attempt to access another user's resource (read or write), the server should continue to return 404 for the same cases it does now. If current code returns 404 for unauthorized access by regular users, maintain that behavior; do NOT change it to 403.
5) If the codebase contains a pathway that currently returns a 403 to regular users for other-users' resources, do not switch any of those pathways to return 403 as part of your changes. If you encounter such pathways and they conflict with the stated acceptance conditions, escalate to the product/architects rather than guessing corrective behavior.
6) Remove or update any server-side errors/messages that specifically indicate the superuser is read-only for other-users' resources. Replace with success responses when the superuser is authorized and operation succeeds. Do not change other error messages unrelated to this role or these operations.
7) Implement automated tests covering these scenarios (unit and integration tests):
   - Superuser attempts to PATCH/PUT/DELETE another user's resource: request succeeds (expected 200/204 as per existing API conventions).
   - Regular user attempts to GET another user's resource (if current behavior is 404): remains 404.
   - Regular user attempts to PATCH/DELETE another user's resource: remains 404 (not 403).
   - Superuser GET (read-all) remains unchanged.
8) Ensure API contract stability: do not change endpoint paths, request/response payload shapes, or status code conventions except where necessary to allow the superuser modify/delete (use existing success codes for modify/delete). Avoid introducing new status codes for the same scenarios.
9) Coordinate with frontend implementer to confirm that the frontend will enable edit/delete controls only when backend accepts those actions; if necessary, provide a short list of endpoints and expected status codes for modify/delete so frontend can assert behavior (do not invent names; list actual endpoints discovered in code review).

Acceptance criteria for backend (must be verifiable):
- A superuser can successfully modify and delete resources owned by other users (verified by automated tests and integration tests).
- Regular users attempting to access other-users' resources continue to receive 404s in the same situations as before; there is no regression to 403.
- Superuser read behavior is unchanged.
- No other roles’ permissions have been widened or altered beyond the stated scope.

Notes to implementer (do not assume):
- Before modifying checks, identify canonical representation of the superuser claim/flag in auth tokens/session; confirm its name rather than guessing.
- If there are policy files or centralized authorization services, prefer updating the policy in the single canonical place rather than patching multiple handlers.
- If resolving a conflict between current code paths and the acceptance conditions would require broader contract decisions (e.g., changing how 404 vs 403 is used globally), stop and escalate—do not guess a global policy change."
  }
}
